title: A transit agency's bus fleet

blocks.text: A transit agency reviews its bus fleet once a year. For each bus the plan picks one of four options: `"keep"` it as it is, `"refurbish"` it, replace it with a `"diesel"` bus, or replace it with an `"electric"` one. The model in `fleet.py` has a binary `y[bid, option]` for every bus and every option. The rules:

items: **One option per bus.** Every bus gets exactly one of the four options; "keep" is a decision like the others.
**Chargers.** The depot has `chargers` charging bays, so at most that many buses can be replaced with electric ones.
**Age.** A bus older than `max_age` years may not be kept: it must be refurbished or replaced. A bus exactly `max_age` years old may still be kept.

blocks.text: Write `add_fleet_rules(model, y, buses, chargers, max_age)` so that the model allows exactly the plans that keep the three rules.
The model so far, with $`B`$ the buses and $`O`$ the four options:
Name the remaining parameters (each bus's age, the chargers, the age limit) and the set of buses too old to keep, then write your rows, each with its quantifier and a label, before you code them.
The tests fix every `y[bid, option]` through its bounds and ask the solver whether the model accepts the plan, so any correct formulation passes. About eight lines.

cases.says: a plan with one option per bus is allowed, and a bus given two options is refused
electric buses up to the charger count are allowed, and one more is refused
keeping a bus older than the limit is refused
a plan that leaves a bus with no option at all is refused
a bus exactly at the age limit may still be kept

origin.section: Doing Nothing Is an Alternative Too, and It Has a Price

concepts: the options for one asset share one row over every start variable of every member
an explicit keep variable turns the group row into an equality and carries the risk of leaving the asset
